title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to test whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks; 3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic validator/emulator as ground truth, we observed no verifier rejections: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); bounded repair was never invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p=1.0; bootstrap resamples=10,000, seed=1729). Crucially, the preregistered shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per paired task and therefore the verifier/repair path was not exercised; this design choice and its statistical consequences are stated explicitly in the abstract and are discussed in the paper. All preregistration, execution traces, validator/scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes are released (see execution/*; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e…; master prompt archived provenance/master_prompt.txt SHA‑256 1872df1e18…). We interpret this artifact‑backed null result in light of generation semantics, task difficulty, verifier design, and bounded repair budget and outline reproducible next steps.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Natural‑language intent→configuration pipelines driven by large language models (LLMs) can simplify network operations but pose correctness and safety risks: stochastic generation may produce syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe device commands. A pragmatic operational architecture is Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR): the LLM generates a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier rejects unsafe candidates, and a repair loop attempts bounded automated fixes using verifier diagnostics. Research question. We preregistered and executed a confirmatory paired experiment to answer: does embedding a deterministic formal network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded GVR loop (bounded repair: ≤1 repair attempt per rejected candidate) increase detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improve bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation? Key methodological constraint (preregistered and decisive). The experiment used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false): for each task the same single generated candidate was evaluated under both arms (baseline and guarded). This preregistered choice produced one generation per paired task (model_calls_used=270) and is the reason the verifier/repair path was never invoked in the observed run; we therefore frame the empirical claim precisely as measuring the verifier’s marginal effect conditional on the same generated candidate, not as a general test of verifier utility under independently sampled stochastic generation.
sections.related_work: Positioning. Our work intersects (1) Generate–Verify–Repair architectures for deterministic validation of stochastic generation (e.g., Cadenas’ GVR framing [doi:10.2139/ssrn.6754899]), (2) network‑configuration formal verification and quantitative verification frameworks (e.g., NetKAT/Weighted NetKAT work [doi:10.1145/3808318]) and (3) recent LLM‑for‑NetOps agentic/intent‑translation studies (surveys and applied systems; see evidence bundle). Unlike bench‑marking papers that compare many language models on knowledge tasks, we executed a preregistered, artifact‑backed operational experiment that places a deterministic verifier in the decision loop and reports exact per‑call traces and validator judgments.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design freeze. The design was preregistered (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Paired design: N=270 distinct intent→configuration tasks (3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks). Validation subset: a preregistered 20% stratified sample (54 tasks) reserved for verifier‑vs‑emulator concordance checks. Model and prompts. Generator: gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses). Model configuration is archived (execution/model_configuration.json, SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820). The exact initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Generation semantics. Per the preregistration we used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation=false): the same generated candidate was used for baseline and guarded arms for each task. This design decision was preregistered and is the primary reason the verifier/repair path could be inactive if the generator proposes correct candidates. Verifier and emulator. Ground truth: a deterministic netops validator/emulator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implemented in Dockerized Kathará/Mininet checked intent constraints and simulated device state; validator traces and scoring JSONs are archived under execution/scoring/. Intervention/budget. Guarded arm: generate → verifier; if verifier rejects, invoke bounded repair loop (max 1 repair call per rejected candidate). Baseline: single‑shot generation evaluated by the same verifier; both arms use the same shared candidate (so no extra model calls per pair). Analysis plan. Primary test: paired binary comparison (exact McNemar two‑sided). Paired‑bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed=1729). All analysis code and outputs archived (analysis/*). Contamination, reproducibility, and logging. Deterministic SHA‑256 snapshotting of prompts, candidates, provider traces, and artifacts prevented silent contamination; execution manifest contains a full per‑artifact hash manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json).
sections.results: Execution and accounting (artifact facts). Planned episodes: 540 (270 pairs). Completed episodes: 540; failed episodes: 0. Model calls used: 270 (one shared generation per pair because of shared_initial_candidate semantics); maximum_model_calls per preregistration = 540. Representative artifact pointers (examples): execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt SHA‑256 f8de4d6e..., execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 350bfaa2.... Primary outcomes (artifact‑backed numbers). Baseline (single‑shot) verifier‑accepted initial candidates: 270/270 = 100%. Guarded (generate → verifier → optional bounded repair) verifier‑accepted final output: 270/270 = 100%. Verifier rejects of initial candidate: 0/270. Bounded repair calls invoked (guarded arm): 0. Repair successes conditional on initial reject: 0/0 (no repairs attempted). Validation subset (preregistered 54 tasks): verifier–emulator concordance = 54/54 (false_accept=0, false_reject=0). Statistical inference (preregistered analysis executed as specified). Paired contingency: n11=270, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Estimated paired difference = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples; seed=1729). Interpretation of these statistics in context. The observed contingency is degenerate: zero discordant pairs. Because the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced a single generated candidate per pair (the same candidate evaluated in both arms), there was no between‑arm generation variability to produce discordant outcomes; consequently (a) the verifier/repair pipeline was never exercised, and (b) the paired statistical test and bootstrap CI are numerically degenerate (p=1.0, CI [0.00,0.00]) and uninformative about verifier utility under independent stochastic generation. This is an artifact‑backed fact: model_calls_used=270 and n_10=n_01=0 are recorded in the deterministic reconciliation and analysis artifacts (execution/* and analysis/*).
sections.discussion: Primary scientific reading. Under the exact preregistered conditions (shared_initial_candidate semantics, gpt-5-mini, the provided synthetic task suite, a conservative single‑repair budget, and the chosen deterministic verifier) the generated candidates were verifier‑acceptable for every task, so inserting the verifier produced no measurable marginal effect. This outcome is an artifact‑backed null result and must be interpreted with the preregistered generation semantics in mind. Why this null occurred and what it does not show. The null result arises from the conjunction of (A) shared_initial_candidate semantics (one generated candidate per pair) and (B) the generator producing verifier‑acceptable candidates for these synthetic tasks at the chosen model settings. It does not show that a verifier is unnecessary in general. In practical deployments, generation variability (independent resampling or nonzero temperature), adversarial or out‑of‑distribution intents, less conservative verifier rule sets, larger repair budgets, or different LLMs can produce verifier rejections that trigger repairs. Statistical implications and preregistered power. The preregistered power/MDE calculation targeted a detectable paired difference of ≈0.10 under assumptions of between‑condition variability; those assumptions do not hold when the experiment uses shared_initial_candidate semantics and the generator produces identical acceptable candidates across arms. Thus the planned power calculation does not apply to the observed degenerate contingency. This is an execution‑artifact fact (see analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and execution/execution_manifest.json). Operational implications and reproducible next steps (artifact‑anchored). To evaluate verifier utility under more aggressive/stochastic generation regimes we recommend reproducible follow‑ups that (each fully verifiable): (1) set independent_condition_generation=true so each arm receives an independent generation (doubling model calls), (2) vary sampling temperature and sampling seeds to expose stochastic failure modes, (3) expand task difficulty and include adversarial/OOD intents, (4) test multiple LLMs and multiple verifier rule‑sets (conservative ↔ permissive), and (5) increase the bounded repair budget (multi‑attempt). All artifacts produced here (preregistration, per‑call traces, scoring JSONs, and hash manifest) enable exact replication and deterministic recomputation of these follow‑ups.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑backed paired experiment that integrated a deterministic network verifier as an oracle in an LLM GVR pipeline. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen model/settings, the generator produced verifier‑acceptable candidates for every one of N=270 tasks; verifier rejects and bounded repairs did not occur, producing a measured paired difference of 0.00 (95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). This artifact‑grounded null result demonstrates the importance of generation semantics and sampling variability in studies that aim to measure verifier utility: in regimes where the generator consistently produces acceptable candidates, an inserted verifier will not change outcomes. We release the full preregistration, execution traces, validator/scoring JSONs, and hash manifest to enable deterministic replication and to support follow‑ups that vary generation semantics, sampling, models, verifier conservative/permissive settings, and repair budgets. Null results with full provenance help identify the experimental regimes where operational interventions change behavior and where they do not; they therefore guide reproducible prioritization of subsequent evaluation work.

Adapter and execution family: hosted_netops_gvr_v1 executed in scientific_confirmatory mode per the preregistration (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration JSON SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). No human manually edited or rewrote manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock. Preregistration and freeze: the experimental plan (sampling, estimands, generation_semantics, retry policy, analysis plan, multiplicity plan, and contamination procedures) was frozen before observing outcomes; preregistration artifact SHA‑256 above. Generation semantics and their effect: the preregistered and executed design used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false), producing one generated candidate per paired task; this is the principal design reason model_calls_used=270 and why the verifier/repair path was not invoked in the observed run. Verifier and emulator: a deterministic netops validator/emulator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implemented in Dockerized Kathará/Mininet provided ground truth; scoring JSONs and validator traces are archived in execution/scoring/ (representative artifact execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json SHA‑256 350bfaa2eec0deb0e16121f5e7effa2d8743d28f3f014856107acfabbb42d87e). Execution manifest and hashes: execution/execution_manifest.json contains full per‑artifact SHA‑256 hashes and provider‑call logs; representative artifacts cited in the manuscript include execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 f8de4d6e...), execution/scoring/task-000001-guarded.json (SHA‑256 350bfaa2e...), and the full hash manifest is available in the evidence bundle. Limits: the study used a single generator (gpt-5-mini), synthetic task bank, a single deterministic verifier, shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, and a bounded repair budget (≤1 repair attempt). These methodological choices and their consequences are declared and discussed in the manuscript. Availability: all preregistration, execution traces, scoring artifacts, and the full hash manifest are released with the manuscript (see execution/* and analysis/*; execution_manifest contains exact paths and SHA‑256 values).
limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments.
Single‑model evaluation: only gpt-5-mini was tested; results do not imply multi‑model generality.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per pair, thereby eliminating between‑arm sampling variability and preventing the verifier/repair path from being exercised; the primary power/MDE calculation assumed between‑condition variability and thus does not apply to the observed degenerate contingency.
Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate; multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated and could change outcomes.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: we tested a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); different verifier conservatism or rule‑sets may change false‑accept/reject trade‑offs and observed utility.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on heterogeneous vendor devices or live production networks.
